title: A finite-length module has a filtration with simple quotients
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $M$ an $R$-module of finite length, i.e. $\mathrm{length}_R(M)<\infty$ [def-weil-pbc-module-length]. Then there are an integer $r\ge0$ and $R$-submodules $0=M_0\subsetneq M_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq M_r=M$ such that each quotient $M_i/M_{i-1}$ ($1\le i\le r$) is simple [def-weil-pbc-simple-module]: it is nonzero and has no $R$-submodule other than $0$ and itself.

source.place: Algebra, Definition Tag 02LY (definition-length, line 12350), Definition Tag 00J1 (definition-simple-module, line 12508) and Lemma Tag 00J3 (lemma-simple-pieces, line 12546, part (2) and the first sentence of its proof): a maximal chain in a finite-length module has simple successive quotients

proof.text: Choose a chain of maximal length. Let $\ell=\mathrm{length}_R(M)<\infty$ [def-weil-pbc-module-length]. Let $S$ be the set of integers $n\ge0$ for which there is a chain of $R$-submodules $0=M_0\subsetneq M_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq M_n=M$. $S$ is nonempty: if $M=0$ the one-term chain $0=M_0=M$ gives $0\in S$, and if $M\ne0$ the chain $0\subsetneq M$ gives $1\in S$. Every $n\in S$ satisfies $n\le\ell$ by the definition of $\ell$ as the supremum. So $S$ is a nonempty set of integers bounded above by $\ell$ and has a largest element $r$; fix a chain $0=M_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq M_r=M$ realizing it. (Stacks says 'choose any maximal chain'; this step writes out why one exists: a chain of largest length cannot be refined.)

Inserting $N$ gives a chain $0=M_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq M_{i-1}\subsetneq N\subsetneq M_i\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq M_r=M$ with $r+1$ proper inclusions, so $r+1\in S$, contradicting the maximality of $r$.
